role: Senior Staff Geologist, mineral exploration company (Douglas, Arizona)
stance_basis: letter explicitly requests that mineral exploration ORV use be excluded from the Executive Order's implementation
summary: W. C. Walker, Senior Staff Geologist writing from Douglas, Arizona, argues that Executive Order 11644 should not apply to off-road vehicles used in mineral exploration, citing the mining law's requirement that public lands remain open for mineral exploration. He contends that the permit system and public participation requirements would be burdensome and expensive for the mining industry, and that restricting ORV use would hinder essential exploration access for men and equipment.
complaint_summary: Walker argues that the Departmental implementation of Executive Order 11644 should specifically exclude ORV use in mineral exploration, as such restrictions would be contrary to mining law, impose burdensome public participation requirements on the mining industry, and hinder essential exploration access.

statement.text:
Please consider the following statement in connection with the above draft:
Since Executive Order 11644 was issued in February, 1972, there has been no interpretation of its effect on the use of off-road vehicles in the exploration for minerals, including oil, non-metallics, and metallics. Of particular interest is the possible effect on the use of the equipment essential for subsurface exploration. In general, this equipment is carried on off-road vehicles, and a proper field procedure usually requires use on a regular grid pattern, which is, of course, compatible only with off-road use.
The intent of Executive Order 11644 appears to be to limit indiscriminate use of off-road vehicles, but it is so broad that it may apply to off-road use of vehicles in connection with the exploration for mineral deposits. This possible application would be contrary to the requirements of the mining law that the public lands shall be open for mineral exploration and location.
The Departmental implementation of the Executive Order should specifically not include the use of off-road vehicles used in connection with the exploration for mineral deposits.
On page 10, lines 5 and 6 up from the bottom, say: "Public participation will be solicited on each area prior to its designation as open (with controls) or closed to ORV use." Attempts to participate in all such areas of interest will be extremely time consuming, expensive, and burdensome to people in the mining industry. The burden of attempting to make presentations on proposed wilderness withdrawals is already overwhelming. It would be desirable to exclude

ORV use by the mineral industry from the provisions of the order.
32
On page 24, paragraph VI, states: "Interior bureaus have major responsibilities for the long term stewardship of the soil, water, mineral, wildlife, vegetative, and natural or historic resources of the Nation." It is probably not desirable to incorporate renewable resources, nonrenewable resources, and esthetic resources in one statement, for the stewardship implication is different for each. For the first, it implies development of a policy of use that maintains and improves them. For the second, it implies recognition of the nonrenewable nature of mineral deposits and the need for the proper and orderly development of them. For the third, stewardship implies protection and preservation.
The present emphasis on environment tends to neglect the essential need for development of the nonrenewable resources. There can be no development without a discovery, and there can be no discovery without exploration. There can be no exploration without access for men and equipment.
The first annual report of the Secretary of the Interior has just been released. One of the points made in this report is that exploration in the United States does not seem to be keeping pace with the nation's growing needs for minerals. Present land use philosophies and withdrawals are hampering the effort at present. Restrictions on the use of off-road vehicles would greatly hinder exploration work.
Very truly yours,
W. C. Walker
Senior Staff Geologist
